claim: Gisting trains an LM to compress a prompt into a few gist tokens whose activations are cached and reused.
quote: gisting, which trains an LM to compress prompts into smaller sets of "gist" tokens which can be cached and reused for compute efficiency

claim: Gist models are learned by modifying Transformer attention masks during ordinary instruction finetuning; no extra training cost.
quote: Gist models can be trained with no additional cost over standard instruction finetuning by simply modifying Transformer attention masks to encourage prompt compression

claim: Tokens after the gist tokens are masked from seeing the prompt, forcing prompt information into the gist prefix.
quote: The model is then restricted such that input tokens after the gist tokens cannot attend to any of the prompt tokens before the gist tokens

claim: What is trained: one new gist token (vocabulary and embedding row) is added and the LM is instruction-finetuned with the gist mask; the paper does not say whether this is full finetuning or parameter-efficient.
quote: we add a single gist token g to the model vocabulary and embedding matrix

claim: The gist prefix is predicted by the (finetuned) LM itself, so a gist prefix is only meaningful to that same gist model (inferred from mechanism).
quote: using the LM itself as the gist predictor G

claim: Base models: LLaMA-7B (decoder-only, ~7B) and FLAN-T5-XXL (encoder-decoder, 11B).
quote: we experiment with LLaMA- 7B [33], a decoder-only GPT-style model with ~7B parameters, and FLAN-T5-XXL [8], an encoder- decoder T5 model [28] with 11B parameters

claim: Output form: the key/value activations of the LM on top of the gist tokens (a Transformer prefix), cached and reused.
quote: G(t) will be the key/value activations on top a set of gist tokens, smaller than the number of tokens in t, yet still inducing similar behavior from the LM

claim: The paper does not discuss closed/API LLMs. Its method requires finetuning the LM itself and consuming its KV activations (inferred from mechanism: not usable with an API-only model); retrofitting a frozen LM is listed only as future work.
quote: another exciting approach is to retrofit an existing, frozen LM by training a smaller model to compress prompts, if finetuning the larger LM is inconvenient

claim: Headline: up to 26x prompt compression, up to 40% FLOPs reduction, 4.2% wall-time speedup, with minimal loss in output quality (authors' abstract).
quote: gisting enables up to 26x compression of prompts, resulting in up to 40% FLOPs reductions, 4.2% wall time speedups, and storage savings, all with minimal loss in output quality

claim: The compression factor is the average prompt length of the validation split divided by the number of gist tokens, so it depends on how short the prompts are.
quote: Compression factors are calculated by computing the average token length of the validation split and dividing by the number of gist tokens

claim: Compressed prompts are short instructions: the average training prompt is ~20 tokens and ~26 tokens in the Human split, so the 26x figure applies to very short instructions, not documents.
quote: the average training prompt has ~20 tokens, compared to ~26 in the human split

claim: Authors state the 26x figure is for unseen out-of-distribution prompts while maintaining output quality.
quote: Gist models can compress unseen OOD prompts up to 26x while maintaining output quality

claim: Number of gist tokens k was varied (Figure 3 axes show 1, 2, 5, 10); models were insensitive to k and a single gist token did not substantially underperform larger prefixes; the single-token model is used for all later experiments.
quote: Models were generally insensitive to the number of gist tokens k: compressing prompts into a single token prefix did not substantially underperform larger prefixes

claim: Too many gist tokens can hurt (LLaMA-7B with 10 gist tokens).
quote: having too many gist tokens hurts performance in some cases (e.g. LLaMA-7B, 10 gist tokens)
